Real people appear only as generic picture-book figures; the mark appears only as loose hand-drawn crayon curves, never the official artwork or wordmark.

lines: This is a true story about a squiggle.
A little curved line, that you have almost certainly seen today.
It began with two runners, in Oregon.
In nineteen sixty-four, a running coach named Bill Bowerman,
and a runner he had once coached, named Phil Knight,
started a tiny company called Blue Ribbon Sports.
For about seven years, they sold running shoes from Japan.
Somebody else's shoes, with somebody else's mark on the side.
Then they decided to make shoes of their own.
And their own shoes would need their own mark.
Phil Knight also taught accounting, at Portland State University.
There, he met a graphic design student named Carolyn Davidson.
He hired her to draw charts and pictures for his company,
In nineteen seventy-one, he asked her for something harder.
A mark, for the side of the new shoes.
And it must not look like the three stripes on another company's shoes.
Which is tricky, when a shoe mostly sits still.
So Carolyn drew on thin tissue paper, laid over a drawing of a shoe.
A line here. A curve there.
She brought at least six designs to Phil and his team.
They chose one. A curve like a tick, like something moving fast.
And what did Phil Knight say?
I don't love it, he said.
But maybe it will grow on me.
When the work was done, Carolyn sent in her bill.
Seventeen and a half hours, at two dollars an hour.
She has said she really worked longer than that.
The shoes needed a name, too. Phil liked Dimension Six.
An early employee, Jeff Johnson, suggested Nike,
the Greek goddess of victory. He said the name came to him in a dream.
On the eighteenth of June, nineteen seventy-one, the curve was used on a product for the very first time.
And a year later, at the Olympic track trials in Eugene, Oregon,
runners laced up a new shoe, with the curve on its side.
The little company grew, and grew, and grew.
In nineteen eighty-three, Phil Knight gave Carolyn a gold ring, shaped like her curve, with a diamond in it.
And five hundred shares of the company. After splits, those became thirty-two thousand.
For years, the mark was printed with the word Nike beside it.
Then, in nineteen ninety-five, the word was taken away.
The curve stood all on its own.
A mark, after all, is only a shape.
What filled it with meaning were the runners.
Years of running, and racing, and winning.
Seventeen and a half hours. Thirty-five dollars.
And a little curve, that grew on everyone.
And that is the end of the story.
